A judge has ruled Donald Trump's lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service manipulated the justice system. (AP: Alex Brandon)

US President Donald Trump's lawsuit against his own government over leaked tax records was an unparalleled exercise in self-dealing, a US judge has said in a scathing ruling.

District Judge Kathleen Williams accused Mr Trump and his legal team of having manipulated the justice system when he sued the nation's revenue collection agency, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS).

The lawsuit ended in a settlement that granted Mr Trump immunity from tax audits and established a $US1.776 billion ($2.56 billion) fund for ‌victims of alleged government "weaponization".

Here's what to know about the controversial lawsuit, which sparked allegations of corruption, and the Judge Williams ruling.

Nearly every president since Richard Nixon has voluntarily released their tax records.

It shows voters they pay taxes and allows them to weigh how a president's personal finances might influence their decisions in office.

Mr Trump became the only exception to that tradition when he refused to release his records as promised during his first term as president.

But in 2020, a contractor leaked more than two decades of his tax information to the press.

Donald Trump has been the only president not to release his tax records since the tradition began. (Reuters: Cheriss May)

On January 29, a year after his return to the Oval Office, Mr Trump sued the IRS, alleging it should have done more to prevent the contractor from accessing his tax returns.

In doing so, Mr Trump became the first sitting US president to sue his own administration.

It was privately settled out of court.

The US president has abandoned plans for a $2.51 billion "anti-weaponization" fund for ‌victims of alleged government "weaponization", according to the acting attorney-general.

As part of a settlement, it was agreed the Department of Justice (DOJ) would set up a pool of taxpayer money that critics argued would be controlled by his allies, from which they could dole out payments to those who said they had suffered "weaponization or lawfare" by the US government.

It also gave Mr Trump immunity from future tax audits.

Both of these terms were highly controversial, with politicians and advocacy groups describing the settlement as an act of blatant corruption.

After widespread backlash and the filing of several lawsuits, the Trump administration ditched plans to move forward with the Anti-Weaponization Fund a fortnight after they were announced.

Mr Trump dropped the lawsuit on May 18.

Back in May, Judge Williams ordered Mr Trump's lawyers to respond to "grievous allegations" made by critics of the settlement that the president abandoned his case to avoid the court's scrutiny of an illegal deal.

She gave them until June 12 to respond in writing to allegations of collusion and whether the case should be reopened because the court was the "victim of fraud".

Now, we've received her ruling on the matter.

In short, she ruled the lawsuit was filed for an "improper purpose" to "manipulate the judicial process".

"The nature of the suit itself and the conduct of the Parties and counsel from its filing make plain that this was an attempt to use the Court to provide some legitimacy to an agreement to confer immunity to people and entities affiliated with the President and to earmark billions of dollars from American taxpayers to redress grievances not defined in the law," she wrote.

It boiled down to a question of whether Mr Trump could legitimately sue himself.

In this case, Mr Trump was not only the plaintiff, but the defendant (having been president, and therefore, in charge of the IRS, at the time of the leak and at the time the lawsuit was filed).

Judge Williams pointed to comments made by acting attorney-general Todd Blanche during a congressional testimony in early June, in which he revealed the fund was no longer moving forward.

Though nothing had been filed in court, Mr Blanche appeared confident in his testimony that he "could speak for, and bind, both sides of this matter", Judge Williams said.

She wrote that this demonstrated "there was only one party whose interests were being represented throughout this case" and concluded the parties were not truly adverse, which is a necessary prerequisite for legal action.

"President Trump did not pursue his claims until he once again occupied the White House and had appointed his former lawyer, and the former lawyer of persons who are putative beneficiaries of the 'Anti-Weaponization Fund' to prominent positions in the DOJ," she wrote.

"These officials then negotiated on behalf of the United States, with his current lawyers, including his former White House Counsel to reach a 'settlement'."

While she stopped short of explicitly voiding the deal shielding Mr Trump from tax scrutiny, she said the government could not claim in official proceedings that the settlement agreement was the result of a legitimate legal process, and that it had "no viable basis in law or fact".

The judge also raised possible disciplinary action against the lawyers involved.

Alejandro Brito, an attorney for Mr Trump who filed the case, was referred for possible disciplinary action before the state bar in Florida.

Another lawyer, Daniel Epstein, was barred from filing lawsuits in the Southern District of Florida for up to a year.

Judge Williams also ordered her ruling be sent to the state bars in New York and the District of Columbia, where ethics complaints have been filed against Mr Blanche and Associate Attorney-General Stanley Woodward.

Mr Blanche has been the acting attorney-general since April, when Mr Trump sacked his predecessor, Pam Bondi.

To fill the position more permanently, he needs to go through the Senate confirmation process, which kicks off this week with Judiciary Committee hearings scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday.

Todd Blanche will appear before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Wednesday, local time. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

The Judiciary Committee will vote on whether to send the nomination to the full Senate.

It would take just one no vote from the GOP to deadlock the committee and effectively sink Mr Blanche's nomination.

And according to the New York Times, there are already some doubts on the Republican side over Mr Blanche.

The former prosecutor is facing multiple ethics complaints over alleged misconduct and abuse of investigative powers during his tenure at the Department of Justice.

Here, Judge Williams's ruling could install another hurdle.
